title: Universal Exception Handlers Swallowing Fatal Failures
pattern: A top-level or library wrapper surrounds all execution paths with a universal "catch-all" exception block to prevent any panic/crash, silently continuing execution with fallback state.
why_bad: While locally giving the illusion of a highly robust system that "never crashes," it is an anti-pattern. If a system runs out of memory (OOM), out of storage space, or hits a corrupted memory invariant, catching and swallowing the error keeps the process alive in a zombie state. The handler itself might try to allocate memory (which will fail), and the program will enter an infinite error loop. It is always better to fail-fast.
detection: A top-level catch-all block swallowing serious, unrecoverable system failures (e.g., OOM, heap exhaustion) or globally suppressing compiler/runtime panics, without immediately terminating the process.
counterexample: Catching recoverable transaction-level errors (like a parsed socket timeout) is valid. Mark `Context-dependent`.
source: John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design*, Chapter 10 "Define Errors Out Of Existence" (p. 48) / Heather Adkins et al., *Building Secure and Reliable Systems*, Chapter 13 "Designing for Defense" (p. 221).
